verses.zh: 耶稣又对门徒说：「绊倒人的事是免不了的；但那绊倒人的有祸了。
verses.en: Jesus[NOTE:1] said to his disciples, “Stumbling blocks are sure to come, but woe[NOTE:2] to the one through whom they come!
notes: Grk “He”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity. Here δέ (de) has not been translated.
See Luke 6:24-26.

verses.zh: 就是把磨石拴在这人的颈项上，丢在海里，还强如他把这小子里的一个绊倒了。
verses.en: It would be better for him to have a millstone[NOTE:1] tied around his neck and be thrown into the sea[NOTE:2] than for him to cause one of these little ones to sin.[NOTE:3]
notes: This term refers to the heavy upper stone of a grinding mill (L&N 7.70; BDAG 660 s.v. μυλικός). sn The punishment of drowning with a heavy weight attached is extremely gruesome and reflects Jesus’ views concerning those who cause others who believe in him to sin.
Grk “if a millstone were tied…and he were thrown.” The conditional construction in Greek has been translated by English infinitives: “to have…and be thrown.”

Or “to stumble.” This verb, σκανδαλίσῃ (skandalisē), has the same root as the noun σκάνδαλον (skandalon) in 17:1, translated “stumbling blocks”; this wordplay is difficult to reproduce in English. It is possible that the primary cause of offense here would be leading disciples (“little ones”) astray in a similar fashion.

verses.zh: 你们要谨慎！若是你的弟兄得罪你，就劝戒他；他若懊悔，就饶恕他。
verses.en: Watch[NOTE:1] yourselves! If[NOTE:2] your brother[NOTE:3] sins, rebuke him. If[NOTE:4] he repents, forgive him.
notes: It is difficult to know if this looks back or forward or both. The warning suggests it looks back. For this verb, see Luke 8:18; 12:1, 15; 20:46; 21:8, 34. The present imperative reflects an ongoing spirit of watchfulness.
Both the “if” clause in this verse and the “if” clause in v. 4 are third class conditions in Greek.

Here the term “brother” means “fellow believer” or “fellow Christian” (cf. BDAG 18 s.v. ἀδελφός 2.a, contra BDAG 19 s.v. 2.c), but with a familial connotation. It refers equally to men, women, or children. However, because of the familial connotations, “brother” has been retained in the translation here in preference to the more generic “fellow believer” (“fellow Christian” would be anachronistic in this context).
Grk “And if.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.

verses.zh: 倘若他一天七次得罪你，又七次回转，说：『我懊悔了』，你总要饶恕他。」
verses.en: Even if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times returns to you saying, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive[NOTE:1] him.”
notes: You must forgive him. Forgiveness is to be readily given and not withheld. In a community that is to have restored relationships, grudges are not beneficial.

verses.zh: 使徒对主说：「求主加增我们的信心。」
verses.en: The[NOTE:1] apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith!”[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “And the.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
The request of the apostles, “Increase our faith,” is not a request for a gift of faith, but a request to increase the depth of their faith.

verses.zh: 主说：「你们若有信心像一粒芥菜种，就是对这棵桑树说：『你要拔起根来，栽在海里』，它也必听从你们。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] the Lord replied,[NOTE:2] “If[NOTE:3] you had faith the size of[NOTE:4] a mustard seed, you could say to this black mulberry[NOTE:5] tree, ‘Be pulled out by the roots and planted in the sea,’[NOTE:6] and it would obey[NOTE:7] you.
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of previous action(s) in the narrative.
Grk “said.”
This is a mixed condition, with ἄν (an) in the apodosis.
Grk “faith as,” “faith like.”
A black mulberry tree is a deciduous fruit tree that grows about 20 ft (6 m) tall and has black juicy berries. This tree has an extensive root system, so to pull it up would be a major operation.

The passives here (ἐκριζώθητι and φυτεύθητι, ekrizōthēti and phuteuthēti) are probably a circumlocution for God performing the action (the so-called divine passive, see ExSyn 437-38). The issue is not the amount of faith (which in the example is only very tiny), but its presence, which can accomplish impossible things. To cause a tree to be uprooted and planted in the sea is impossible. The expression is a rhetorical idiom. It is like saying a camel can go through the eye of a needle (Luke 18:25).
The verb is aorist, though it looks at a future event, another rhetorical touch to communicate certainty of the effect of faith.

verses.zh: 你们谁有仆人耕地或是放羊，从田里回来，就对他说：『你快来坐下吃饭』呢？
verses.en: “Would any one of you say[NOTE:1] to your slave[NOTE:2] who comes in from the field after plowing or shepherding sheep, ‘Come at once and sit down for a meal’?[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “Who among you, having a slave…would say to him.”
See the note on the word “slave” in 7:2.

Grk “and recline at table,” as 1st century middle eastern meals were not eaten while sitting at a table, but while reclining on one’s side on the floor with the head closest to the low table and the feet farthest away. See BDAG 70 s.v. ἀναπίπτω 1.

verses.zh: 岂不对他说：『你给我预备晚饭，束上带子伺候我，等我吃喝完了，你才可以吃喝』吗？
verses.en: Won’t[NOTE:1] the master[NOTE:2] instead say to him, ‘Get my dinner ready, and make yourself ready[NOTE:3] to serve me while[NOTE:4] I eat and drink. Then[NOTE:5] you may eat and drink’?
notes: The question includes a Greek particle, οὐχί (ouchi), that expects a positive reply. The slave is expected to prepare a meal before eating himself.
Grk “he”; the referent has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “and gird yourself” (with an apron or towel, in preparation for service).
BDAG 423 s.v. ἕως 2.b, “to denote contemporaneousness as long as, while…w. subjunctive…Lk 17:8.”
Grk “after these things.”

verses.zh: 仆人照所吩咐的去做，主人还谢谢他吗？
verses.en: He won’t thank the slave because he did what he was told,[NOTE:1] will he?[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “did what was commanded.”
The Greek construction anticipates a negative reply which is indicated in the translation by the ‘tag’ at the end, “will he?” Thanks are not required.

verses.zh: 这样，你们做完了一切所吩咐的，只当说：『我们是无用的仆人，所做的本是我们应分做的。』」
verses.en: So you too, when you have done everything you were commanded to do, should say, ‘We are slaves undeserving of special praise;[NOTE:1] we have only done what was our duty.’”[NOTE:2]
notes: Some translations describe the slaves as “worthless” (NRSV) or “unworthy” (NASB, NIV) but that is not Jesus’ point. These disciples have not done anything deserving special commendation or praise (L&N 33.361), but only what would normally be expected of a slave in such a situation (thus the translation “we have only done what was our duty”).
Or “we have only done what we were supposed to do.”

verses.zh: 耶稣往耶路撒冷去，经过撒马利亚和加利利。
verses.en: Now on[NOTE:1] the way to Jerusalem,[NOTE:2] Jesus[NOTE:3] was passing along[NOTE:4] between Samaria and Galilee.
notes: Grk “Now it happened that on.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.

For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.sn This is another travel note about Jesus going to Jerusalem in Luke 9:51-19:48, the so-called “Jerusalem journey” section of Luke’s Gospel. It is not a straight line journey because to travel along the Galilean and Samaritan border is to go east or west, not south to Jerusalem.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “was traveling about.”

verses.zh: 进入一个村子，有十个长大麻疯的，迎面而来，远远地站着，
verses.en: As[NOTE:1] he was entering[NOTE:2] a village, ten men with leprosy[NOTE:3] met him. They[NOTE:4] stood at a distance,
notes: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
The participle εἰσερχομένου (eiserchomenou) is taken temporally.

The ten men with leprosy would have been unable to approach Jesus (Lev 13:45-46; Num 5:2-3). A leper was totally ostracized from society until he was declared cured (Lev 13:45-46). For more on the condition, see the note on lepers in Luke 4:27.
Grk “leprosy, who.” Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, the relative pronoun was replaced with a personal pronoun and a new sentence started at this point in the translation.

verses.zh: 高声说：「耶稣，夫子，可怜我们吧！」
verses.en: raised their voices and said, “Jesus, Master, have mercy[NOTE:1] on us.”
notes: “Have mercy on us” is a request to heal them (Luke 18:38-39; 16:24; Matt 9:27; 15:22; 17:15; 20:31-32; Mark 10:47-49).

verses.zh: 耶稣看见，就对他们说：「你们去把身体给祭司察看。」他们去的时候就洁净了。
verses.en: When[NOTE:1] he saw them he said, “Go[NOTE:2] and show yourselves to the priests.”[NOTE:3] And[NOTE:4] as they went along, they were cleansed.
notes: Καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.

The participle πορευθέντες (poreuthentes) is a good example of an adverbial participle of attendant circumstance. As such, it picks up the force of an imperative from the verb to which it is related (ExSyn 640-45).
These are the instructions of what to do with a healing (Lev 13:19; 14:1-11; Luke 5:14).

Grk “And it happened that as.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.

verses.zh: 内中有一个见自己已经好了，就回来大声归荣耀与　神，
verses.en: Then one of them, when he saw he was healed, turned back, praising[NOTE:1] God with a loud voice.
notes: Grk “glorifying God.”

verses.zh: 又俯伏在耶稣脚前感谢他；这人是撒马利亚人。
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] fell with his face to the ground[NOTE:2] at Jesus’ feet and thanked him.[NOTE:3] (Now[NOTE:4] he was a Samaritan.)[NOTE:5]
notes: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “he fell on his face” (an idiom for complete prostration).
And thanked him. This action recognized God’s healing work through Jesus.
Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the introduction of a parenthetical comment.

This is a parenthetical note by the author. The comment that the man was a Samaritan means that to most Jews of Jesus’ day he would have been despised as a half-breed and a heretic. The note adds a touch of irony to the account (v. 18).

verses.zh: 耶稣说：「洁净了的不是十个人吗？那九个在哪里呢？
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] Jesus said,[NOTE:2] “Were[NOTE:3] not ten cleansed? Where are the other[NOTE:4] nine?
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “Jesus answering said”; this is redundant in contemporary English and has been simplified in the translation.
The Greek construction used here (οὐχί, ouchi) expects a positive reply.
The word “other” is implied in the context.

verses.zh: 除了这外族人，再没有别人回来归荣耀与　神吗？」
verses.en: Was no one found to turn back and give praise to God except this foreigner?”[NOTE:1]
notes: Jesus’ point in calling the man a foreigner is that none of the other nine, who were presumably Israelites, responded with gratitude. Only the “outsiders” were listening and responding.

verses.zh: 就对那人说：「起来，走吧！你的信救了你了。」
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] he said to the man,[NOTE:2] “Get up and go your way. Your faith has made you well.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “to him”; the referent has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Or “has delivered you”; Grk “has saved you.” The remark about faith suggests the benefit of trusting in Jesus’ ability to deliver. Apparently the Samaritan benefited from the healing in a way the other nine did not.

verses.zh: 法利赛人问：「　神的国几时来到？」耶稣回答说：「　神的国来到不是眼所能见的。
verses.en: Now at one point[NOTE:1] the Pharisees[NOTE:2] asked Jesus[NOTE:3] when the kingdom of God[NOTE:4] was coming, so he answered, “The kingdom of God is not coming with signs[NOTE:5] to be observed,
notes: The words “at one point” are supplied to indicate that the following incident is not necessarily in chronological sequence with the preceding event.
See the note on Pharisees in 5:17.

Grk “having been asked by the Pharisees.” The passive construction has been translated as an active one in keeping with contemporary English style, and the direct object, Jesus, has been supplied from the context.

The kingdom of God is a major theme of Jesus’ teaching. The nature of the kingdom of God in the NT and in Jesus’ teaching has long been debated by interpreters and scholars, with discussion primarily centering around the nature of the kingdom (earthly, heavenly, or both) and the kingdom’s arrival (present, future, or both). An additional major issue concerns the relationship between the kingdom of God and the person and work of Jesus himself. See Luke 6:20; 11:20; 17:20-21.

Or “is not coming in a way that it can be closely watched” (L&N 24.48). Although there are differing interpretations of what this means, it probably refers to the cosmic signs often associated with the kingdom’s coming in the Jewish view (1 En. 91, 93; 2 Bar. 53–74). See D. L. Bock, Luke (BECNT), 2:1412-14, also H. Riesenfeld, TDNT 8:150.

verses.zh: 人也不得说：『看哪，在这里！看哪，在那里！』因为　神的国就在你们心里（心里：或译中间）。」
verses.en: nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ For indeed, the kingdom of God is[NOTE:1] in your midst.”[NOTE:2]
notes: This is a present tense in the Greek text. In contrast to waiting and looking for the kingdom, it is now available.

This is a far better translation than “in you.” Jesus would never tell the hostile Pharisees that the kingdom was inside them. The reference is to Jesus present in their midst. He brings the kingdom. Another possible translation would be “in your grasp.” For further discussion and options, see D. L. Bock, Luke (BECNT), 2:1414-19.

verses.zh: 他又对门徒说：「日子将到，你们巴不得看见人子的一个日子，却不得看见。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] he said to the disciples, “The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days[NOTE:2] of the Son of Man, and you will not see it.
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.

This is a reference to the days of the full manifestation of Jesus’ power in a fully established kingdom. The reference to “days” instead of “day” is unusual, appearing only here and in v. 26, but it may be motivated merely by parallelism with the “days” of Noah there and the “days of Lot” in v. 28.

verses.zh: 人将要对你们说：『看哪，在那里！看哪，在这里！』你们不要出去，也不要跟随他们！
verses.en: Then people[NOTE:1] will say to you, ‘Look, there he is!’[NOTE:2] or ‘Look, here he is!’ Do not go out or chase after them.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “And they will say.” The plural in Greek is indefinite, referring to people in general. Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
The words “he is” here and in the following clause are understood and have been supplied from the context.
Do not go out or chase after them. There will be no need to search for the Son of Man at his coming, though many will falsely claim its arrival.

verses.zh: 因为人子在他降临的日子，好像闪电从天这边一闪直照到天那边。
verses.en: For just like the lightning flashes[NOTE:1] and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.[NOTE:2]
notes: The Son of Man’s coming in power will be sudden and obvious like lightning. No one will need to point it out.

Some very significant mss (P75 B D it sa) lack the words ἐν τῇ ἡμέρα αὐτοῦ (en tē hēmera autou, “in his day”), but the words are included in א A L W Θ Ψ ƒ1,13 M lat sy bo. On the one hand, the shorter reading is impressive because it has some of the best Alexandrian and Western witnesses in support; on the other hand, the expression ἐν τῇ ἡμέρα αὐτοῦ is unusual (found nowhere else in the NT), and may be considered the harder reading. A decision is difficult, but it is probably best to retain the words. NA28 rightly has the words in brackets, expressing doubt as to their authenticity.

verses.zh: 只是他必须先受许多苦，又被这世代弃绝。
verses.en: But first he must[NOTE:1] suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.
notes: The Son of Man’s suffering and rejection by this generation is another “it is necessary” type of event in God’s plan (Luke 4:43; 24:7, 26, 44) and the fifth passion prediction in Luke’s account (9:22, 44; 12:50; 13:32-33; for the last, see 18:32-33).

verses.zh: 挪亚的日子怎样，人子的日子也要怎样。
verses.en: Just[NOTE:1] as it was[NOTE:2] in the days of Noah,[NOTE:3] so too it will be in the days of the Son of Man.
notes: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Or “as it happened.”
Like the days of Noah, the time of the flood in Gen 6:5-8:22, the judgment will come as a surprise as people live their day to day lives.

verses.zh: 那时候的人又吃又喝，又娶又嫁，到挪亚进方舟的那日，洪水就来，把他们全都灭了。
verses.en: People[NOTE:1] were eating,[NOTE:2] they were drinking, they were marrying, they were being given in marriage—right up to the day Noah entered the ark. Then[NOTE:3] the flood came and destroyed them all.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “They.” The plural in Greek is indefinite, referring to people in general.
These verbs (“eating…drinking…marrying…being given in marriage”) are all progressive imperfects, describing action in progress at that time.
Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Like that flood came and destroyed them all, the coming judgment associated with the Son of Man will condemn many.

gr.gloss: they were being given in marriage

verses.zh: 又好像罗得的日子；人又吃又喝，又买又卖，又耕种又盖造。
verses.en: Likewise, just as it was[NOTE:1] in the days of Lot, people[NOTE:2] were eating, drinking, buying, selling, planting, building;
notes: Or “as it happened.”
Grk “they.” The plural in Greek is indefinite, referring to people in general.

verses.zh: 到罗得出所多玛的那日，就有火与硫磺从天上降下来，把他们全都灭了。
verses.en: but on the day Lot went out from Sodom,[NOTE:1] fire and sulfur rained down from heaven and destroyed them all.[NOTE:2]
notes: And destroyed them all. The coming of the Son of Man will be like the judgment on Sodom, one of the most immoral places of the OT (Gen 19:16-17; Deut 32:32-33; Isa 1:10).

Most of the roofs in the NT were flat roofs made of pounded dirt, sometimes mixed with lime or stones, supported by heavy wooden beams. They generally had an easy means of access, either a sturdy wooden ladder or stone stairway, sometimes on the outside of the house.

verses.zh: 人子显现的日子也要这样。
verses.en: It will be the same on the day the Son of Man is revealed.

verses.zh: 当那日，人在房上，器具在屋里，不要下来拿；人在田里，也不要回家。
verses.en: On that day, anyone who is on the roof,[NOTE:1] with his goods in the house, must not come down[NOTE:2] to take them away, and likewise the person in the field must not turn back.
notes: The swiftness and devastation of the judgment will require a swift escape. There is no time to come down from one’s roof and pick up anything from inside one’s home.
An allusion to Gen 19:26. The warning about Lot’s wife is not to look back and long to be where one used to be. The world is being judged, and the person who delays or turns back will be destroyed.

verses.zh: 你们要回想罗得的妻子。
verses.en: Remember Lot’s wife![NOTE:1]
notes: Or “tries to preserve”; Grk “seeks to gain.”

verses.zh: 凡想要保全生命的，必丧掉生命；凡丧掉生命的，必救活生命。
verses.en: Whoever tries to keep[NOTE:1] his life[NOTE:2] will lose it,[NOTE:3] but whoever loses his life will preserve it.
notes: Grk “soul.” See the discussion of this Greek term in the note on “life” in Luke 9:24.

The Greek word translated life can refer to both earthly, physical life and inner, transcendent life (one’s “soul”). In the context, if a person is not willing to suffer the world’s rejection and persecution in order to follow Jesus but instead seeks to retain his physical life, then that person will lose both physical life and inner, transcendent life (at the judgment). On the other hand, the one who willingly gives up earthly, physical life to follow Jesus (“loses his life”) will ultimately preserve one’s “soul” (note that the parallel in John’s Gospel speaks of “guarding one’s ‘soul’ for eternal life” (John 12:25).

There is debate among commentators and scholars over the phrase one will be taken and the other left about whether one is taken for judgment or for salvation. If the imagery is patterned after the rescue of Noah from the flood and Lot from Sodom, as some suggest, the ones taken are the saved (as Noah and Lot were) and those left behind are judged. The imagery, however, is not directly tied to the identification of the two groups. Its primary purpose in context is to picture the sudden, surprising separation of the righteous and the judged (i.e., condemned) at the return of the Son of Man.

verses.zh: 我对你们说，当那一夜，两个人在一个床上，要取去一个，撇下一个。
verses.en: I tell you, in that night there will be two people in one bed; one will be taken and the other left.[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “at the same place.” According to L&N 46.16, this refers to a hand mill normally operated by two women.

verses.zh: 两个女人一同推磨，要取去一个，撇下一个。（有古卷加：
verses.en: There will be two women grinding grain together;[NOTE:1] one will be taken and the other left.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Several mss (D ƒ13 [579] 700 al lat sy) add (with several variations among these witnesses) 17:36 “There will be two in the field; one will be taken and the other left.” It is not well enough attested to be original. Further, it is an assimilation to the parallel in Matt 24:40, which marks the addition as secondary. The present translation follows NA28 in omitting the verse number, a procedure also followed by a number of other modern translations.
Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.

verses.zh: 两个人在田里，要取去一个，撇下一个。）」
门徒说：「主啊，在哪里有这事呢？」耶稣说：「尸首在哪里，鹰也必聚在那里。」
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] the disciples[NOTE:2] said[NOTE:3] to him, “Where,[NOTE:4] Lord?” He replied to them, “Where the dead body[NOTE:5] is, there the vultures[NOTE:6] will gather.”[NOTE:7]
notes: Grk “they”; the referent (the disciples, v. 22) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “answering, they said to him.” This is redundant in contemporary English and has been simplified in the translation.
The question “Where, Lord?” means, “Where will the judgment take place?”
Or “corpse.”

Jesus’ answer is that when the judgment comes, the scenes of death will be obvious and so will the location of the judgment.tn The same Greek term can refer to “eagles” or “vultures” (L&N 4.42; BDAG 22 s.v. ἀετός), but in this context it must mean vultures because the gruesome image is one of dead bodies being consumed by scavengers.
Grk “will be gathered.” The passive construction has been translated as an active one in English.
